AFG.story:
Most of Afghanistan's record concerns the sexual abuse of boys by armed men who hold power. The main form is bacha bazi, in which powerful men keep boys to dance for them and sexually abuse them. In 2014 the Afghanistan Independent Human Rights Commission, the country's official human rights body, held hearings in 17 provinces. Two-thirds of the victims said the men paid them. The commission's chair, Sima Samar, said the law did not properly prevent the practice.

Many of the abusers were commanders in the state's own forces, and the foreign governments that armed them kept paying for them. In 2015 The New York Times reported that US soldiers had been told to ignore the abuse of boys by their Afghan allies, in some cases on US bases. The Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction (SIGAR), a US watchdog, reported that as of August 2016 the Pentagon was tracking 75 gross human rights violations by Afghan security forces from 2010 to 2016, at least seven of them child sexual assault. A US law, the Leahy Law, requires aid to units that commit such abuses to be cut. The Pentagon used an exception in that law to keep supporting the units, and in December 2015 approved continued funding for 12 units implicated in 14 violations.
Under the Taliban's de facto government the abuse is recorded in the institutions it runs. The UN verified sexual violence against 12 children in 2023, 10 of the cases attributed to the Taliban, and the abduction of 3 children by the Taliban for sexual violence; it verified 13 cases in 2022 and 6 in 2024. In 2024 boys aged 10 to 17 told Radio Azadi, the Afghan service of the US-funded broadcaster RFE/RL, that teachers in Taliban-run madrasahs (religious schools) pressured them into sexual acts. One boy reported a teacher to the school's senior religious teacher, who only told the teacher to stop. A UN report counted 6,836 Taliban-established madrasahs for boys in 2024.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scores Afghanistan's human trafficking market at 9 out of 10. The US State Department places it in Tier 3, its lowest rank.

Abuse of boys by men with armed or official power is recorded under both the former government and the Taliban. SIGAR wrote that the full extent of child sexual assault by Afghan security forces "may never be known".

BEN.story:
The material gathered for this map records one form of child exploitation in Benin, and its source is mainly about Benin's neighbours. Under trokosi, traditional shrines take girls, usually young virgins, as atonement for a relative's alleged wrongdoing. The girls serve the shrine priests without pay, and in most shrines sexual service to the priest is treated as a duty; defenders of the practice deny this. The source places trokosi among the Fon people in Benin as well as the Ewe in Ghana and Togo. Ghana made ritual servitude a crime in 1998. The material records no law or prosecution against it in Benin.

The other figures cover all forms of exploitation. Walk Free, an anti-slavery research group, estimated 37,000 people in modern slavery in Benin in 2023, 3 per 1,000 people, adults and children together. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scores the human trafficking market at 6 out of 10. The US State Department places Benin in Tier 2, for governments that do not fully meet its minimum standards against trafficking but are making significant efforts. Technology companies sent 16,950 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse located in Benin to the US CyberTipline in 2024, 117.2 per 100,000 people. Childlight, a research centre, found no representative survey data on online child abuse for West and Central Africa.

How many girls are held at shrines in Benin, and whether the state has acted against the practice, is not recorded.

BRA.story:
Brazil's record centres on the sale of children for sex along its highways and in its coastal tourist cities, and on the local politicians, businessmen and clergy who took part in it. The Federal Highway Police and the charity Childhood Brasil assessed more than 9,700 truck stops, bars, motels and other roadside points in 2021–2022 and rated 640 critical. An earlier survey found that 38% of the victims came from elsewhere and had possibly been trafficked. In coastal tourist destinations, the US State Department's 2025 report says taxi drivers and hotel, bar and nightclub staff arrange the sale of children to visitors, and it cites a study suggesting that up to 16 per cent of girls aged 14–17 in one northeastern metropolitan area were likely victims of commercial sexual exploitation.

Congress has three times investigated the people who profit. A joint commission of senators and deputies (CPMI) in 2004 put more than 250 people on notice, among them 20 serving politicians, including three mayors, about 30 businessmen and five priests. A Chamber of Deputies inquiry in 2014 asked for the indictment of 37 people, including the mayor of Coari in Amazonas, Adail Pinheiro, and a serving state deputy.

In the cases on record, prosecutions of officials stalled. The 2025 US report said no investigations of complicit officials were reported. Luiz Afonso Sefer, a state deputy in Pará, was convicted in 2010 of raping a child; the case has since been overturned, reinstated and annulled on appeal, and as of February 2026 his 20-year sentence had not been carried out. Brazil has the largest Catholic population in the world and no national inquiry into abuse in institutions. Church cases reach court one at a time; in 2011 a judge in Arapiraca convicted three priests of the Diocese of Penedo of abusing altar boys, and the victims said the bishop had known.

The inquiries changed the law. The 2004 commission's bill became Law 12.015 of 2009, and laws passed during the Senate's 2008–2010 inquiry into paedophilia made possession of abuse material a crime and ordered the closure of businesses where children were exploited. That inquiry also got Google to lift secrecy on pages of its Orkut social network linked to child abuse.

Roadside and tourist exploitation was still reported in 2025. In the one case on record where a politician was convicted, the sentence had not been carried out by February 2026.

CMR.story:
The material for this map records one form of child sexual abuse in Cameroon, sexual violence against girls by armed men, including the state's own soldiers. The UN verified sexual violence against 17 girls in Cameroon in 2023. It attributed 10 of the cases to the Cameroon Armed Forces, 6 to unidentified perpetrators and 1 to JAS, the faction of Boko Haram that operates across the Lake Chad basin. In 2024 it verified sexual violence against 6 girls, one of them by the armed forces, and the abduction of 50 children.

These counts include only the cases the UN could verify. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scores Cameroon's human trafficking market at 6.5 out of 10 and its state-embedded criminal actors, people inside the state who take part in organised crime, at 8.5. Walk Free, an anti-slavery research group, estimated 155,000 people in modern slavery in 2023. Technology companies sent 25,169 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse located in Cameroon to the US CyberTipline in 2024. Childlight, a research centre, found no representative survey data on online child abuse for West and Central Africa.

In 2023 the armed forces were the largest group of perpetrators in the cases the UN verified. The material records no prosecution of soldiers.

DJI.story:
Djibouti appears in the record for this map as a destination for girls from Ethiopia. The US State Department's 2025 report says traffickers exploit Ethiopian girls in domestic servitude and sex trafficking in neighbouring countries, particularly Djibouti and Sudan, sometimes using drugs to control them, and that reports of official complicity continued. The report is about Ethiopia and does not say who in Djibouti takes part.

Djibouti's own figures are small and cover all forms of exploitation. Walk Free, an anti-slavery research group, estimated 7,000 people in modern slavery in 2023, 7.1 per 1,000 people. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scores the human trafficking market at 7 out of 10. The US State Department places Djibouti on its Tier 2 Watch List, the rank above its lowest. Technology companies sent 509 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse located in Djibouti to the US CyberTipline in 2024. Childlight, a research centre, found no representative survey data on online child abuse for the Middle East and North Africa.

How many Ethiopian girls are held in Djibouti, and by whom, is not recorded.

ETH.story:
Ethiopia's record has three parts. The largest is the sending of children abroad for adoption with false papers. The others are girls taken across the borders for domestic work and sex, and sexual violence against girls in the war in Tigray.

Orphanages and foreign agencies ran the adoptions. Adoptions abroad rose from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008. Ethiopia sent 33,303 children abroad from 2003 to 2022, and the US issued 15,166 immigrant visas to children adopted from Addis Ababa from 1994 to 2014; many others went to Spain, France and Italy. Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive. The US State Department found one agency, Better Futures Adoption Services, involved in child trafficking, and it lost its Ethiopian licence in 2011. A Flemish investigation of adoptions from 1997 to 2015 found that the true story sometimes differed from the files and that in the worst cases the birth parents had not given the children up voluntarily.

The receiving countries stopped first. Ireland suspended adoptions from Ethiopia in 2007, Australia in 2009 and Denmark in 2016. Ethiopia suspended foreign adoptions in November 2017, and parliament banned adoption by foreigners from 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect of adopted children abroad.

Girls are also moved out of the country for work. The US State Department's 2025 report says traffickers exploit Ethiopian girls in domestic servitude and sex trafficking in Djibouti and Sudan, sometimes using drugs to control them, and that begging rings exploit Ethiopian women and children in Saudi Arabia. It says reports of official complicity continued.

In the Tigray war, from 2020, forces on several sides committed sexual violence against girls. The International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia, appointed by the UN, documented rapes by Tigrayan forces of girls as young as 11 in Amhara villages in 2021, alongside widespread sexual violence by Ethiopian and Eritrean forces in Tigray. The BBC reported in February 2021 that 200 girls under 18 had registered at health facilities in Mekelle as rape survivors. The UN verified sexual violence against 73 children in Ethiopia in 2024 and attributed 38 cases to the Ethiopian National Defence Force, the national army.

Adoption abroad has been banned since 2018. The trafficking of girls to neighbouring countries and sexual violence by the army were still reported in 2024 and 2025.

GIN.story:
The two forms of child sexual abuse documented in Guinea both took place in institutions run by outsiders, aid agencies in refugee camps and a missionary boarding school.

In early 2002 a joint mission of the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) and the charity Save the Children UK reported that refugee children in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were being sexually exploited by employees of aid groups, UNHCR and other UN bodies, and by peacekeepers, often in exchange for food and aid. The UN's internal investigators, the Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS), fully investigated 43 cases and substantiated 10. They included the rape of a 14-year-old refugee girl in a Guinean camp and a UN Volunteer's sexual relationship with a girl of about 15 in Guéckédou. OIOS found no allegation against a UN staff member substantiated and said it found no evidence of "widespread" abuse; Save the Children UK replied that nothing the UN found made it think it was wrong. The one substantiated case against a peacekeeper ended with his repatriation. The UN can only send peacekeepers home, and prosecuting them is left to the countries that sent them.

Mamou Alliance Academy boarded the children of missionaries of the Christian and Missionary Alliance (C&MA), a church denomination, working in West Africa. Former pupils wrote to the denomination's headquarters about abuse for about ten years before an inquiry was set up in response to 30 alumni. The independent commission heard 80 testimonies and in 1998 found the denomination negligent. It identified nine offenders, and the abuse included sexual molestation and rape. The C&MA's US board asked victims' forgiveness in an open letter.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scores Guinea's state-embedded criminal actors, people inside the state who take part in organised crime, at 8 out of 10 and its resilience to organised crime at 2.96. The US State Department places Guinea in Tier 2.

Both findings are more than twenty years old. The material for this map holds no later record of abuse in Guinea's camps or schools, and Childlight, a research centre, found no representative survey data on online child abuse for West and Central Africa.

HKG.story:
The material for this map records Hong Kong mainly as a place where child sexual abuse material was stored online. The Internet Watch Foundation (IWF), a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, ranked Hong Kong the third or fourth largest host of the material it acted on in 2023 and 2024. The figure the map uses for 2023 to 2025 is 24,063. In 2025 the amount fell sharply. The record does not say which companies hosted it or why it fell.

Hong Kong also made sexual offences against children committed abroad punishable at home. The Prevention of Child Pornography Ordinance of December 2003 gave 24 sexual offences extraterritorial effect, meaning they can be prosecuted in Hong Kong when committed elsewhere. The record has no case brought under it.

Hong Kong is listed among the places involved in Project Spade, the Toronto police investigation into Azov Films, a company that sold films of child exploitation to more than 50 countries and led to 348 arrests in 2013. The record does not say what part Hong Kong played.

Technology companies sent 17,357 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse located in Hong Kong to the US CyberTipline in 2024, 230.7 per 100,000 people. The US State Department places Hong Kong on its Tier 2 Watch List, the rank above its lowest.

Hosting of abuse material in Hong Kong fell in 2025. Who hosted it, and whether anyone was prosecuted, is not recorded.

IRN.story:
The research for this map found no documented case, network or flow of child sexual abuse or trafficking in Iran. Childlight, a research centre that combines surveys into global estimates, found no representative survey data on online child abuse for the Middle East and North Africa.

The measures that exist are outside ratings of trafficking and slavery of all kinds. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scores Iran's human trafficking market at 8 out of 10 and its state-embedded criminal actors, people inside the state who take part in organised crime, at 9.5. The US State Department places Iran in Tier 3, its lowest rank. Walk Free, an anti-slavery research group, estimated 597,000 people in modern slavery in 2023, 7.1 per 1,000 people, adults and children together. Technology companies sent 83,405 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse located in Iran to the US CyberTipline in 2024.

How much of this involves children, and in what forms, is not documented in the material for this map.

JPN.story:
Most of Japan's record concerns adults who held power over children's careers, religious life or care, and long delays before complaints were acted on. The largest case is in the entertainment industry. An external investigation for Johnny & Associates, the country's dominant agency for boy bands, found in August 2023 that its founder, Johnny Kitagawa, had sexually abused minors who wanted to be pop singers for decades; the BBC summarises the finding as abuse of hundreds of boys and young men. The first press report appeared in 1965. After Kitagawa sued the magazine Shūkan Bunshun, courts upheld its reporting of the abuse in 2003 and 2004, yet Japanese media barely covered it. Journalists attributed this to the agency's control over bookings of its performers. Kitagawa died in 2019 and was never charged.

Action came after a BBC documentary and a former trainee's public allegations in 2023. The company admitted the abuse, and by August 2026 its successor, Smile-Up, had decided to compensate 585 people.

Church and children's home records are smaller. A survey of all 16 Catholic dioceses, published in 2020, found 16 cases of sexual abuse of minors from the 1950s to the 2010s, and most victims took 10 to 30 years to report. Eight accused clerics were transferred, and some who were punished kept working or moved to another diocese. A Yomiuri Shimbun survey found at least 47 staff at children's homes confirmed to have committed indecent acts against 69 children in the five years to fiscal 2020.

A commercial market also sells girls' company. In the "JK business", JK meaning high-school girl, shops sell simulated dates and services with high-school girls. Police counted 91 such shops at the end of 2024. The US State Department's 2025 report says these and "compensated dating", often tied to organised crime, are used for sex trafficking of Japanese children and of children from China, South Korea, Laos, the Philippines, Singapore and Vietnam.

Since 1999 Japanese nationals can be prosecuted for child prostitution and child pornography offences abroad. In June 2023 Japan raised the age of consent from 13 to 16 and extended the deadline for prosecuting rape from 10 to 15 years. The survivor group Spring said this was not enough.

Kitagawa's victims are being compensated through Smile-Up, and JK shops were still operating at the end of 2024. The church and children's home figures include only cases those institutions confirmed.

LBR.story:
Liberia's record comes from the years of civil war and after it, when many children depended on armed groups, aid agencies and orphanages. Three forms are documented there, sexual exploitation by aid workers and peacekeepers, fraud in adoption through private orphanages, and war crimes aided by the country's own president.

In early 2002 a joint mission of the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) and the charity Save the Children UK reported that refugee children in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were being sexually exploited by employees of aid groups and UN bodies, and by peacekeepers, often in exchange for food and aid. The UN's internal investigators substantiated 10 of the 43 cases they fully investigated across the region. The UN's tables for 2024 still list two child victims connected to its mission in Liberia, UNMIL. About 750 paternity claims against peacekeepers have been made since 2006, and more than 500 are still pending; the UN refers them to the countries that sent the troops, most of which have not taken meaningful action.

After the war ended in 2003, the number of private orphanages rose from 40 to 120. Private orphanages and adoption facilitators supplied the children adopted abroad. In 2005 the Hannah B. Williams Orphanage in Monrovia was closed and 89 of its 102 "orphans" were returned to their families. A 2007 report by UNICEF and the adoption agency Holt International found that many children entered adoption through fraud, including false promises to birth parents, and the UN mission found unaccredited for-profit orphanages. The US issued 1,553 visas to children adopted from Monrovia from 1994 to 2014. Canada placed a moratorium on Liberian adoptions.

Charles Taylor, the former president of Liberia, was convicted in 2012 by the Special Court for Sierra Leone of aiding and abetting crimes by the Revolutionary United Front, a rebel force in Sierra Leone's civil war. These included sexual slavery and the use of children under 15 as fighters. He was sentenced to 50 years.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scores Liberia's state-embedded criminal actors at 7.5 out of 10. The US State Department places Liberia on its Tier 2 Watch List.

Canada's moratorium is the only restriction on Liberian adoptions in the record. Most paternity claims against peacekeepers remain pending.

MDV.story:
The research for this map found no documented case, network or flow of child sexual abuse or trafficking in the Maldives. The one large figure comes from technology companies, which sent 4,161 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse located in the Maldives to the US CyberTipline in 2024, 788.4 per 100,000 people. These reports locate the account that uploaded or shared the material; they do not show where the children were.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scores the human trafficking market at 6.5 out of 10, and the US State Department places the Maldives on its Tier 2 Watch List. Childlight, a research centre, found no representative survey data on online child abuse for South Asia.

What lies behind the CyberTipline reports is not documented in the material for this map.

MRT.story:
The research for this map found no documented case of child sexual abuse or trafficking in Mauritania. Walk Free, an anti-slavery research group, estimated 149,000 people in modern slavery there in 2023, 32 per 1,000 people. That count covers adults and children and all forms of slavery.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scores the human trafficking market at 7.5 out of 10 and the country's resilience to organised crime at 3.25. The US State Department places Mauritania in Tier 2. Technology companies sent 8,089 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse located in Mauritania to the US CyberTipline in 2024. Childlight, a research centre, found no representative survey data on online child abuse for West and Central Africa.

How many of the people Walk Free counts are children, and whether any are sexually exploited, is not recorded in the material for this map.

NRU.story:
Child sexual abuse is documented on Nauru in one place, the Regional Processing Centre, a detention centre for asylum seekers that the Australian government funded and ran on the island through contracted guards and staff. The guards controlled detainees' daily needs, and the findings describe that control being traded for sex. A review by Philip Moss, commissioned by the Australian government and published in March 2015, was aware of three rape allegations, one involving a minor. It confirmed that a guard demanded to see a female detainee naked in exchange for extra shower time with her young child, and concluded that guards trading marijuana with detainees for sexual favours was possibly occurring.

In April 2015 staff wrote in an open letter that the Australian government had known of alleged abuses against women and children for more than 18 months. The Australian Human Rights Commission's national inquiry, "The Forgotten Children", reported 33 incidents of reported sexual assault in immigration detention, onshore and on Nauru, from January 2013 to March 2014, "the vast majority involving children". A Senate committee reported on the centre in August 2015.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scores its human trafficking market at 1 out of 10, the lowest score.

The findings come from Australian inquiries into a centre Australia ran. The material records no prosecution of guards or staff.

POL.story:
Poland's record centres on Catholic priests who abused children and on bishops who moved them to other parishes after being told. In 2019 the Polish Episcopal Conference, the body of the country's bishops, reported 382 priests accused of abusing 625 children between 1990 and mid-2018. The State Commission on Paedophilia, set up by the government after a 2020 documentary on abuse in the church, studied 345 cases in its first report in 2021. Almost 30% of the perpetrators were clergy and 35% relatives. In its 2022 report, clergy were the largest professional group among abusers who were not relatives.

Bishops handled accused priests by transferring them. An independent commission for the Diocese of Sosnowiec found in February 2026 that bishops had been repeatedly alerted but often took no action, and when they acted they usually moved the priest to another parish. It found at least 50 children harmed and 19 of 23 accused priests confirmed as offenders. The first sanctions on bishops came after the Sekielski brothers' documentaries "Tell No One" (2019) and "Hide and Seek" (2020) led to Vatican investigations. Bishop Edward Janiak of Kalisz resigned in 2020, Archbishop Sławoj Leszek Głódź of Gdańsk was removed the same year, and the Vatican imposed disciplinary measures on Cardinal Henryk Gulbinowicz.

When Polish clergy were accused of abusing children abroad, the Vatican and the lack of an extradition treaty kept them from Dominican courts. Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, the pope's ambassador to the Dominican Republic, was recalled to the Vatican in 2013 before Dominican prosecutors opened an investigation. A church tribunal found him guilty, and he died in 2015 before a Vatican criminal trial. Fr Wojciech Gil, a Polish priest who worked there, returned to Poland, which has no such treaty with the Dominican Republic. Polish police arrested him in 2014 using Dominican evidence, and in 2015 a court in Wołomin sentenced him to seven years for abusing six minors in the Dominican Republic and two in Poland.

Under Nazi occupation from 1940 to 1945, the SS took Polish children judged "racially valuable" and placed them with German families under new identities. Estimates reported by DW run up to 200,000 children. A US military tribunal at Nuremberg convicted 13 officials in 1948.

The State Commission recommended in 2021 that the deadline for prosecuting child sexual abuse be abolished. The Sosnowiec review is the only examination of one diocese's files in the record.

RUS.story:
The largest part of Russia's record concerns Ukrainian children taken during the war in Ukraine. Russia is accused of deporting and transferring Ukrainian children. On 17 March 2023 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia's commissioner for children's rights, for the unlawful deportation and transfer of children. Yale's Humanitarian Research Lab found at least 6,000 Ukrainian children held in at least 43 camps in 2022. Ukraine counts 20,651 children deported or forcibly displaced, of whom 2,752 had returned by October 2026. The UN's Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine found that Russian authorities committed rape and other sexual violence as war crimes, in cases that included children; Ukraine's prosecutor general records 23 children sexually abused.

Before this, Russia was a major source of children for adoption abroad. It sent 59,427 children abroad from 2003 to 2022, and the US issued 60,266 visas to children adopted from Russia from 1994 to 2014. After a US adoptive mother sent a 7-year-old back to Moscow alone in 2010, the Dima Yakovlev Law banned adoption by US citizens from 1 January 2013.

Girls cross Russia's borders in both directions. Amnesty International reported in 2004 that the women and girls trafficked into forced prostitution in Kosovo, where foreign troops and UN staff produced most of the traffickers' income, came mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia. The US State Department's 2025 report says Kazakh women and girls are exploited in Russia.

Russia has also been a base for selling abuse material. Blue Orchid, a Moscow-based site, sold videos of the sexual abuse of boys, some as young as 12, for $200 to $300 each, mostly to customers in the United States. Russian and US police worked together, and by March 2001 five Russians and four US citizens had been arrested. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that removes abuse images, acted on 5,797 internet addresses in Russia, 2% of its total.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scores Russia's state-embedded criminal actors, people inside the state who take part in organised crime, at 9 out of 10. The US State Department places Russia in Tier 3, its lowest rank.

Ukraine was still counting deported children in October 2026. The record for this map notes no trial on the ICC warrants.

SRB.story:
Two things are documented in Serbia. One is the neglect of children and adults with disabilities in state institutions, where investigators found a risk of sexual exploitation. The other is Serbia's place on the route along which women and girls were trafficked into Kosovo.

Mental Disability Rights International (MDRI), an advocacy group, investigated Serbian institutions for four years and reported in 2007 on conditions affecting more than 17,000 people with disabilities. It found children and adults tied to beds or kept in cribs for years, with no oversight, treatment it called "tantamount to torture". At Vršac men and women lived in mixed wards, and staff said they made no effort to find out whether sex was consensual. In 2006 the director of one institution refused to let the investigators see a locked area and asked them to leave, and Serbian officials dismissed the allegations as propaganda.

After NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in Kosovo in 1999, Kosovo became a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution, according to Amnesty International in 2004; the foreign presence produced 80% of the traffickers' income. The women and girls were brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia through Serbia. Amnesty found no evidence of criminal proceedings against any military personnel in their home countries.

Serbia is listed among the countries involved in two international investigations of abuse sites, Dreamboard, closed in 2011, and the streaming platform Kidflix, closed in 2025; the record does not say what part Serbian users or police played. Technology companies sent 15,556 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse located in Serbia to the US CyberTipline in 2024, 236.2 per 100,000 people. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scores Serbia's state-embedded criminal actors at 8 out of 10.

The institutional findings date from 2007. The material for this map holds no later account of whether conditions changed or anyone was held responsible.

TGO.story:
The material gathered for this map records one form of child exploitation in Togo. Under trokosi, traditional shrines among the Ewe people of Ghana and Togo, and the Fon in Benin, take girls, usually young virgins, as atonement for a relative's alleged wrongdoing. The girls serve the shrine priests without pay, and in most shrines sexual service to the priest is treated as a duty; defenders of the practice deny this. Ghana made ritual servitude a crime in 1998. The material records no law or prosecution against it in Togo.

The other figures cover all forms of exploitation. Walk Free, an anti-slavery research group, estimated 28,000 people in modern slavery in Togo in 2023. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scores Togo's state-embedded criminal actors, people inside the state who take part in organised crime, at 7.5 out of 10. The US State Department places Togo in Tier 2. Technology companies sent 6,712 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse located in Togo to the US CyberTipline in 2024. Childlight, a research centre, found no representative survey data on online child abuse for West and Central Africa.

How many girls are held at shrines in Togo is not recorded.

TZA.story:
Two forms of child sexual abuse are documented in Tanzania, the sale of children for sex, centred on Zanzibar and the larger cities, and abuse at a boarding school run by a Catholic order.

The US State Department's 2025 report says traffickers exploit children in Zanzibar in sex trafficking, including by foreign offenders, and in forced labour and domestic servitude. Women and girls from the mainland are brought to Zanzibar with false promises, and child sex trafficking also occurs in Arusha, Dar es Salaam, Dodoma, Mbeya and Mwanza. The report names traffickers, brokers and foster families among those involved, and says the government did not adequately address corruption and official complicity.

In the 1960s four priests of the Institute of Charity, a Catholic order known as the Rosminians, physically and sexually abused boys at St Michael's boarding school in Soni, in what was then Tanganyika. One of them was the English priest Kit Cunningham. The order knew of his abuse before he died in 2010, and that year it refused to pay compensation. The abuse became public through a BBC documentary in June 2011, after which the order acknowledged the crimes and 22 former pupils pursued a compensation claim. The case is recorded as settled.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scores the human trafficking market at 6.5 out of 10, and the US State Department places Tanzania in Tier 2. Technology companies sent 16,917 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse located in Tanzania to the US CyberTipline in 2024, 24.7 per 100,000 people.

Child sex trafficking in Zanzibar and the cities was still reported in 2025. The material for this map holds no inquiry into abuse in Tanzanian institutions.

VNM.story:
Most of Vietnam's record concerns children moved out of the country. They include babies sent for adoption abroad with false papers, girls sold into marriage or brothels in neighbouring countries, and children taken to work in Britain. In the cases on record the children came from poor families and from ethnic minorities in the northern borderlands.

Adoption was the largest flow, and state employees were charged in the biggest case. In 2009 a court in Nam Dinh tried 16 people, including the head of two provincial social welfare centres and doctors and nurses at village clinics, on charges of abuse of power. They were accused of soliciting infants from poor families and falsifying papers to say the babies had been abandoned; 266 babies were sent abroad from 2005 to July 2008. In April 2008 the US embassy reported that recorded desertions had risen 17-fold or more at orphanages in seven provinces, and Vietnam did not renew its adoption agreement with the US when it expired that September. Vietnam sent 14,039 children abroad from 2003 to 2022. France suspended adoptions from Vietnam in 1999, and Flanders stopped them after a review of its adoption system.

Girls are trafficked across land borders. The US State Department's 2025 report says traffickers in border villages lure women and girls, particularly Hmong, to China for forced marriage involving sex trafficking or forced labour, and use "bride kidnapping" against ethnic-minority girls. Most children in the brothels of Svay Pak, near Phnom Penh in Cambodia, were ethnic Vietnamese, many sold by destitute families. In Britain, Vietnamese children are exploited on cannabis farms and in nail salons; 416 were referred to the Home Office as possible victims of modern slavery in 2024, and more than 150 Vietnamese minors had gone missing from UK care by 2017.

Foreign offenders travel to Vietnam. In 2007 an Australian charity found 80 commercial cases of child exploitation by foreigners in Sa Pa, and the Ministry of Public Security set up a unit to investigate child sex tourism. In 2006 a Vietnamese court convicted the British singer Paul Gadd, known as Gary Glitter, of obscene acts with two girls aged 10 and 11, after Cambodia had expelled him.

Vietnam identified 236 child victims of trafficking in 2024. Adoption abroad has been cut back since 2008, while trafficking of girls to China and of children to Britain was still reported in 2024 and 2025.
